clinicalPearls: Presents as tender, indurated, erythematous to violaceous plaques or nodules appearing hours to a couple of days after localised cold exposure
Classically seen on the cheeks of infants after sucking ice lollies ('popsicle panniculitis') because their subcutaneous fat has a higher saturated fat content
In adults it may follow cold exposure of the thighs, as in horse riders in cold weather (equestrian variant)
Lesions arise at sites of direct contact with cold and are usually self-limiting
Biopsy performed early shows a lobular panniculitis, often with a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-subcutaneous junction
The history of preceding cold exposure is the key to diagnosis and avoids unnecessary investigation
Management is reassurance and avoidance of further cold exposure, as lesions resolve spontaneously
reference.pathophysiology: Cold panniculitis is a localised injury to subcutaneous fat provoked by exposure to cold. Adipose tissue with a higher proportion of saturated fatty acids, as in infants, solidifies and is damaged at higher temperatures than adult fat, explaining the predisposition in young children. The cold induces crystallisation and injury of adipocytes with a resulting inflammatory response in the fat lobules. The reaction is self-limited once the cold stimulus is removed, and lesions typically resolve without scarring.
additionalDifferentials: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn
Cold agglutinin or cryoglobulin-related skin disease
additionalInvestigations: Careful history of cold exposure at the affected site
Skin biopsy including subcutaneous fat if the diagnosis is uncertain
Cryoglobulins and cold agglutinins where atypical or recurrent
Full blood count and inflammatory markers to exclude infection
Consideration of underlying cold-sensitivity disorders if lesions are unusually severe
redFlags: Features suggesting cellulitis or abscess requiring antimicrobial treatment
Recurrent or widespread lesions disproportionate to cold exposure
Systemic symptoms or evidence of an underlying cold-sensitivity disorder
Ulceration or necrosis, which is atypical and warrants review
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting; lesions usually resolve over one to a few weeks without scarring once cold exposure ceases. Recurrence can occur with repeated cold contact.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as cellulitis and prescribing unnecessary antibiotics
Failing to elicit the history of cold exposure
Not recognising the higher susceptibility of infants' fat to cold injury
